target.thesis: Human illocutionary force is often settled incrementally through uptake and later ownership, so a force-fixing intention present at output time cannot by itself be what separates human speakers from LLMs. Whether LLMs show reason-responsive taking-up of and commitment to their earlier outputs remains open, and it is a condition on how the system is organised.
target.headline: The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.
target.target: Gubelmann's malfunction test, Attah's pipeline template for communicative intention, and the implicit human paradigm in Barandiaran and Almendros.
target.sketch: Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.

findings.part: The human-side premise. Force is often not fixed by a speaker's output-time communicative intention, but is settled later through the interlocutors' follow-up. This is the premise that retrospective force-fixing is not marginal.
findings.source: Rachel McDonald (author name not shown in the results), "Reimagining Illocutionary Force"
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="29-7">Sometimes the force of an utterance seems to be determined neither at initial performance nor at hearer interpretation, but even later, through negotiations and clarifications by both interlocutors.</cite> The paper's theory <cite index="29-1,29-2">draws on work on adjacency pairs and conversational interaction, and accommodates speaker intentions that may be disjunctive, indeterminate and/or inconsistent over time.</cite>
findings.note: It builds the paper's own theory on late force-fixing and attacks the intention-plus-recognition ('ratification') view, so it looks ENDORSED. I saw only abstract and intro snippets, so PRECEDENT-or-ANTICIPATED is undecided. The negotiating parties it describes are speaker and hearer. It does not say that the speaker's own later ownership or retraction is constitutive, and it has no LLM application.
findings.url_note: The author's name is inferred from the PhilArchive ID (MCDRIF) and the 'McDonald 2021' citation in the results; verify.

findings.part: Constitution by interaction. Force is negotiated or co-constructed in the course of the conversation.
findings.source: McDonald (author name not shown in the results), "Your word against mine: the power of uptake", Synthese, 2020/21
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="31-11">A third theory of uptake holds that hearers and speakers work together to decide upon the utterance's force, negotiating and co-constructing it in the course of the conversation.</cite> The paper sets this aside to compare two other theories of the power of uptake.
findings.note: The view is raised and set aside in a footnote, so it counts as PASSING-to-ENTERTAINED and is credited, not conceded.

findings.part: Empirical grounding that retrospective or sequential force-fixing is not marginal in human talk (conversation analysis, linguistics).
findings.source: Cambridge Elements, "Speech Act Theory", 2025; chapter "Action Ascription in Social Interaction" (Cambridge UP); "The Multiple Accountabilities of Action"
findings.what_they_say: The Elements text reports a conversation-analytic strand on which meaning is <cite index="42-2">co-constructed on the fly through tacit negotiations</cite>, so that intentions may be more of a post facto participant resource (the snippet cuts off mid-quotation). The action-ascription chapter says that <cite index="67-2">intersubjectivity is accomplished sequentially only if the first speaker produces a third-position turn confirming the ascription</cite>. It also says that action is <cite index="67-4">subject to multiple, successive interpretations or drafts</cite>. The Multiple Accountabilities paper says outcomes can <cite index="66-5">reach back over a whole call, retrospectively coloring the meaning of its component actions</cite>.
findings.note: This is usable evidence for the premise and does not rival the thesis. I saw only snippets. The CA work concerns action ascription and repair, not speech-act metaphysics or LLMs.

findings.part: Named target: Gubelmann's malfunction test. Whether the target view is as the thesis describes it, and its organisational ground.
findings.source: Reto Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now)", Philosophy & Technology, 2024 (abstract seen; the malfunction test seen only as quoted by Gordon, "Speech Acts and Large Language Models", PhilArchive preprint)
findings.what_they_say: The abstract says <cite index="56-8,56-9">LLMs cannot act because they lack intentions, since agents with intentions must be autonomous organisms while LLMs are heteronomous mechanisms.</cite> Gordon quotes Gubelmann: <cite index="1-4">unless there is a sensible distinction between an AI system's malfunctioning and its intentionally harming someone, the system lacks coincidence.</cite>
findings.note: The malfunction test is confirmed, but only through a secondhand quote. The ground Gubelmann gives is autonomy, an organisational condition, which sits close to the thesis's closing claim that the condition is about how the system is organised. I did not see his text on whether the intention is a pre-act message or a diachronic pattern, so the thesis's description of him is unverified. This is not an anticipation of the thesis.

findings.part: Named target: Attah's pipeline template for communicative intention. His conclusion also overlaps with the thesis's first clause.
findings.source: Nuhu Osman Attah, "Do language models lack communicative intentions?", Synthese 205(5), 2025
findings.what_they_say: Attah argues that <cite index="11-5,11-6">once we fairly assess LLM and human cognitive architectures there are no good reasons to suppose LLMs lack communicative intentions, so communicative intention is rejected as a ground of the difference between LLMs and humans.</cite> The paper works with Levelt-style components: <cite index="11-11">the Conceptualizer takes into account the discourse context and accumulated knowledge to generate a representation</cite>. A Levelt summary (Scribd, secondhand) says the conceptualizer <cite index="15-2">generates the communicative intention</cite>.
findings.note: The Conceptualizer-then-Formulator template is confirmed from snippets, so the target ascription holds. Attah reaches the same negative conclusion (intention does not separate humans from LLMs) by attributing intentions to LLMs, not by showing that human force-fixing is retrospective. The thesis must distinguish its route from his. This is ADJACENT and not ANTICIPATED because the grounds differ.

findings.part: Named target: the implicit human paradigm in Barandiaran and Almendros. The thesis's description of the target may need repair.
findings.source: Xabier E. Barandiaran & Lola S. Almendros, "Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models", Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences, 2025 (arXiv 2024 preprint also seen)
findings.what_they_say: The abstract calls ChatGPT <cite index="21-4">a library-that-talks, devoid of (autonomous) agency, but capable of engaging performatively on non-purposeful yet purpose-structured and purpose-bounded tasks.</cite> The preprint defines purposeful action as <cite index="27-2">behavior that is imbued with purpose all along its unfolding</cite>. It also says LLMs generate products that <cite index="26-9">recursively shape (through chain-of-thought techniques) their subsequent outputs</cite>.
findings.note: The purposeful versus purpose-structured contrast is confirmed. Their human paradigm is purpose present throughout the unfolding of an action, which is not an output-time message-plus-intention. So 'implicit human paradigm' fits only loosely; I saw only the abstract and snippets of their text. They do not address speech-act force or retrospective ownership.

findings.part: Empirical (cognitive science) treatment of illocutionary force at the level of reply threads, with LLMs used as a control.
findings.source: Zachary P. Rosen & Rick Dale, "LLMs Don't 'Do Things with Words' but Their Lack of Illocution Can Inform the Study of Human Discourse", Proc. Cognitive Science Society, 2024
findings.what_they_say: The study measures <cite index="47-3">how far community members maintain earlier comments' concepts when replying</cite>. It treats the LLM as a control because <cite index="47-6">LLMs inherently lack illocutionary intent</cite>.
findings.note: This is an interaction-structure measure of force-related effects. It assumes that LLMs lack illocutionary intent and does not test taking-up or ownership of the speaker's own earlier outputs. The thesis can use its method but must note the assumption.

findings.part: Rival positions in the LLM speech-act debate that a referee will raise: hearer projection, proxy assertion, normative functionalism.
findings.source: Gordon, "Speech Acts and Large Language Models" (PhilArchive preprint); Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion", Inquiry, 2024; "Who asserts when no one asserts?", Synthese, 2026
findings.what_they_say: Gordon holds that <cite index="1-8">the perlocutionary effect arises because of the hearer's projection of intention</cite>. Williams & Bayne note <cite index="3-2">a strong prima-facie case for treating chatbots as conversational partners capable of assertion</cite> and then survey objections. The 2026 Synthese paper says <cite index="9-3">on the proxy view LLM outputs are taken to have illocutionary force traced to others, though LLMs lack beliefs, intentions and agency.</cite>
findings.note: These are all snippets. None was seen to discuss a diachronic pattern of the speaker owning or retracting earlier outputs as constitutive. The functionalist and normative-status papers are the likeliest place for an unseen overlap, which I could not check.

finding.what_is_left: That human illocutionary force is often settled by later interaction is already argued by McDonald (provisional, from abstract and intro snippets) and is supported by conversation-analytic work. What remains is the claim that this undercuts the use of an output-time force-fixing intention as the human/LLM dividing line in the Gubelmann, Attah and Barandiaran–Almendros discussions. The thesis would argue that the speaker's own taking-up, owning and retracting of earlier outputs is constitutive of force, and that whether LLM threads show this pattern is an open, organisation-level question about interaction structure. I did not find that application in any work I could see.
credit: McDonald 2021 — collaboration theory: force sometimes fixed late by negotiation between speaker and hearer, with intentions indeterminate over time; the thesis adds the speaker's own later ownership and the LLM application
McDonald 2020 — names the constitution/negotiation theory of uptake as a third option

Schegloff, Enfield & Sidnell, Heritage via the action-ascription and accountabilities chapters — third-position confirmation and repair; action subject to successive 'drafts'; retrospective recolouring
Cambridge Elements Speech Act Theory 2025 — reports the conversation-analytic view of intentions as a post facto participant resource
Gubelmann 2024 — an organisational (autonomy) ground for the human/LLM difference, which the thesis's closing claim resembles
Attah 2025 — the same negative conclusion about communicative intention as a dividing line, reached from the LLM side; the Conceptualizer-to-Formulator template
Barandiaran & Almendros 2025 — purposeful versus purpose-structured; purpose throughout the unfolding of an action
Rosen & Dale 2024 — an empirical, thread-level handle on illocutionary force, with LLMs as a control
finding.not_found: The search was thin and mostly saw abstracts and snippets. I did not see full text of Gubelmann, Attah, Barandiaran–Almendros or McDonald, so the extent of each author's endorsement is unconfirmed. I did not find a source on 'discovering force from where an utterance goes', or any work that makes the speaker's own later endorsement or disowning constitutive of force and applies it to LLMs. I did not search the philosophy literature on retrospective or post hoc intention (action theory, interpretivism, Brandom-style scorekeeping), or Levelt's own treatment of incremental production, or the Haugh/Levinson sources behind the 'post facto' snippet. I also did not search empirical work on LLM self-consistency, self-correction, sycophancy, retraction or commitment-tracking across turns. That is the literature most likely to bear on the thesis's empirical question, so the clean results on those topics reflect no search, not an absence of work. I did not find an SEP-style survey of LLMs and speech acts. The newest syntheses I saw (Gvoždiak 2025, Williams & Bayne 2024) were seen only as citations or snippets.

sep.why: The theses concern illocutionary force and communicative intention in LLMs versus humans, so speech-acts is the core debate, intention covers the force-fixing intention claim, and assertion covers commitment, ownership and retraction of earlier outputs.

findings.position: Success of some speech acts depends on audience uptake, so force is not fixed by the speaker's output-time state alone. Austin's felicity conditions are reported with the example of a bet that misfires without uptake.
findings.who: Austin; Langton, Hornsby and Langton (via the silencing discussion)
findings.quote: Other attempts at speech acts might misfire because their addressee fails to respond with an appropriate uptake: I cannot bet you $100 on who will win the election unless you accept that bet.
findings.note: Gives the thesis a base for the claim that force is partly settled after output, but only as a felicity condition for some acts, not as incremental fixing of force.

findings.position: A speaker can later retract or withdraw an earlier speech act, and so is no longer beholden to its commitments. This is a form of post-hoc ownership or disowning of one's earlier act.
findings.who: Sbisà 2007, as reported in the entry
findings.quote: on Wednesday I may be able to retract a claim I made on Monday... I am now no longer beholden to the commitments that the speech acts engender
findings.note: Supports the 'later ownership' element, though the entry treats retraction as undoing commitment, not as settling force.

findings.position: Force is characterised by the normative commitments a speaker overtly undertakes, such as being answerable to 'How do you know?' and being obliged to retract if unable to respond. This is a reason-responsive, commitment-based account that the thesis's 'reason-responsive taking-up of and commitment to' can build on.
findings.who: Green (the entry's own view); Williamson 1996 on challenges
findings.quote: One who asserts P lays herself open to the challenge, 'How do you know that?', and she is obliged to retract P if she is unable to respond to that challenge adequately.
findings.note: Supplies a normative-commitment criterion for what 'ownership' of an output would involve.

findings.position: Force is fixed by the speaker's manifested communicative intention at the time of utterance (Strawson's intentionalism), and speaker meaning is a necessary condition for non-conventional speech acts. This is a rival to the claim that force is often settled incrementally rather than by an output-time intention.
findings.quote: What makes an utterance of a sentence in the indicative mood a prediction rather than a command, for instance, is that it manifests an intention to be so taken
findings.note: The thesis must argue that this account is incomplete. It does not have to deny it, and the entry also says intending is not enough: 'Those intentions must be efficacious.'

findings.position: Some deny that refusal requires uptake, treating it like inviting or surrendering, which can occur whether or not the audience grasps or accepts them. This limits how general an uptake condition on force can be.
findings.quote: Bird (2002) denies that the speech act of refusal requires uptake.
findings.note: A referee would cite this against making uptake a general determinant of force.

findings.position: A speech act can be performed by way of other acts without a distinct intention to perform it, so force need not always trace to one force-fixing intention at output time.
findings.who: Entry's own discussion of illocutionary logic (building on Searle and Vanderveken's strong commitment)
findings.quote: Even in such a case she performs S n only by virtue of intentionally performing some other set of speech acts
findings.note: Weakly suggests that force can outrun the intention behind a particular output, though some intention to perform speech acts is still required.

nearest_positions: Intentionalism about force: force is fixed by the manifested communicative intention, and speaker meaning (overt commitment) is necessary for speech acts — Strawson 1964, Green, Bertolet
Force as overt normative commitment (assertion answerable to 'How do you know?', obligation to retract), with retraction possible later — Green, Williamson 1996, Sbisà 2007

Austin/Searle conventionalism with uptake as a felicity condition, including the silencing literature — Austin, Searle, Langton, Hornsby and Langton, versus Bird 2002 who denies uptake is required for refusal
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Large language models and machine or AI speakers generally, and the contrast between human and artificial speakers. The entry also does not discuss force being settled incrementally across turns, the idea that later taking-up and ownership of an output fixes its force, or reason-responsiveness to one's own earlier outputs as a condition on the speaker's organisation. Nor does it mention any account on which the human/machine difference lies in system organisation instead of in intention at output time.

findings.position: Intention need not be formed before the act. There is intention in action, formed as one acts, as well as prospective intention. The thesis's point that a prior force-fixing intention is not required can build on this.
findings.who: Searle 1983, as reported in the entry; the entry also cites Bratman 2000 for 'intentional action without intention'
findings.quote: I can wave my arm intentionally without planning in advance. This fact elicits a refinement often credited to Searle (1983, pp. 84–5): the distinction between prospective intention and intention in action.
findings.note: This only shows that intention need not precede action. It says nothing about speech acts, force, or uptake.

findings.position: Intending is not a static state present at one moment. It is being in progress towards completing an act, so intentional status can be fixed over time. The thesis's incremental settling of force would apply this kind of view, but the entry never applies it to speech or to later ownership.
findings.who: Thompson 2008; Anscombe-inspired writers (Moran and Stone 2009, Ferrero 2017, Russell 2018)
findings.quote: intending to do A is not a mental state because it is not static; instead it is a form of imperfectivity or being in progress towards the intentional completion of an act
findings.note: The entry presents this as a theory of intention in action generally. The thesis would be an application to illocutionary force, which the entry does not draw.

findings.position: Intention is marked by functional organisation: commitment, resistance to reconsideration, and means-end coherence over time. This backs the thesis's claim that the relevant condition concerns how the system is organised and not a momentary mental state.
findings.who: Bratman 1987, 2009, 2018; the entry also reports the Aristotelian 'commitment' point
findings.quote: intentions are ‘conduct-controlling pro-attitudes, ones which we are disposed to retain without reconsideration, and which play a significant role as inputs to [means-end] reasoning’
findings.note: This is a candidate organisational criterion for the LLM question. The entry says nothing about artificial systems.

findings.position: Acting for a reason involves the agent's having and answering the 'Why?' question about what she is doing, and knowing the reason-giving explanation. This is close to reason-responsive taking-up of one's earlier doings, and a referee would raise it for the thesis's 'ownership' condition.
findings.quote: in acting for a reason, I know an explanation of what I am doing that cites that reason, and therefore know that I am doing it. That is why, for Anscombe, the question ‘Why?’ is ‘given application’ by the agent.
findings.note: The entry treats this as constitutive of intentional action in general, not as a retrospective ownership of outputs.

findings.position: On the orthodox 'Simple View', intentional action requires an intention (in action) whose object is the act, present as the act is done. That would make a time-of-output intention a necessary condition. The entry also reports that the view is open to serious objections, so this is a rival to answer and not a refutation.
findings.who: Searle's refinement, which the entry reports as 'orthodox in action theory'; Bratman names it 'the Simple View' and rejects it
findings.quote: This refinement preserves the idea that doing A intentionally requires an intention whose object is doing A. This is what Bratman (1987, p. 112) has dubbed ‘the Simple View.’
findings.note: The thesis denies only that such an intention suffices to separate humans from LLMs. It does not deny that one is necessary, so the conflict is partial.

nearest_positions: Intending as being in progress / imperfective, not a mental state — Thompson, Moran and Stone, Ferrero, Russell
Intention as plan: commitment, resistance to reconsideration, diachronic coherence — Bratman
Intention in action as a mental state executed in action (Simple View) — Searle, with Davidson and Davis as causal-theory background
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Speech acts, illocutionary force, uptake by an audience, later ownership of earlier utterances, and LLMs or any artificial system. The entry is entirely about intention in action and for the future, and never mentions language use, retrospective settling of what an act was, or AI.

findings.position: Commitment accounts place the normative core of assertion in how the speaker later responds to challenges (defend or retract). Rescorla goes furthest: no norm governs the making of an assertion, only norms governing later reactions. The entry reports this as a commitment account of assertion, not as a claim that force is settled incrementally.
findings.who: Brandom, MacFarlane, Peirce, Alston, Green; Rescorla (2009a)
findings.quote: there is no norm at all for proper making of assertions. There are only norms that govern later reactions. ... he must either defend the assertion or else retract it
findings.note: Supplies the 'later ownership' ingredient, but the entry treats commitment as incurred by the act of asserting, not as settling its force afterwards.

findings.position: Assertoric commitment is partly constituted by reason-responsive conduct over the conversation: answering appropriate challenges, deferring to other sources, or withdrawing. This gives a functional criterion that could be tested on a system's behaviour.
findings.quote: commits the speaker to defend her claim in response to legitimate challenges
findings.note: The thesis can build on this to state what 'reason-responsive taking-up of and commitment to earlier outputs' would involve.

findings.position: Austin held that illocutionary acts depend on securing uptake. The entry also notes that hearer-uptake and other hearer-directed relations bear on assertion, and Hamblin links commitment to what is said next.
findings.quote: it does depend on the hearer's being aware of the utterance and understanding it in a certain way ... 'securing of uptake'
findings.note: Gives a precedent for the uptake side of the thesis. Uptake is not presented as settling force incrementally.

findings.position: Uptake is not necessary for assertion in the speaker-content case. Bill asserted that p even though Lisa had left the room. This cuts against making uptake a condition of force.
findings.who: The entry's own argument against Austin's uptake requirement
findings.quote: Bill still asserted that it was closed, since Bill believed she was still there.
findings.note: The thesis must restrict its claim to the cases where force really is settled post hoc, or answer this point.

findings.position: Commitment is not sufficient for assertion (the 'I hereby commit myself' counterexample). Pagin argues this puts pressure on every hearer-directed or social account. A commitment-based condition on LLMs would therefore not by itself fix assertoric force.
findings.who: Pagin (2004); partial replies by Pegan, MacFarlane, García-Carpintero, Marsili & Green
findings.quote: incurring a commitment is not sufficient for asserting
findings.note: A rival the thesis must answer if it makes ownership or commitment the distinguishing mark.

findings.position: Intention-based accounts make a (reflexive) communicative intention at the time of utterance constitutive of illocutionary force. This is the view the thesis says cannot alone separate humans from LLMs. The entry also reports the regress and sneaky-intention problems for these accounts.
findings.who: Grice (1957), Searle (1969), Bach & Harnish (1979); critics Strawson, Sperber & Wilson
findings.quote: S intends U to produce IE by means of the recognition of i-1
findings.note: The target of the thesis's first clause. The entry's criticisms of intention accounts support part of the thesis.

findings.position: Cognitive safeguards: the hearer meta-represents the speaker's beliefs and intentions and can reject what is said, and social sanctions apply to misleading assertions. These are organisation-level features that distinguish assertion.
findings.quote: it must also be subject to the cognitive and social safeguards that distinguish assertion
findings.note: A nearby functional, system-organisation criterion for assertoric force.

findings.position: Underdetermination of content or force at the time of utterance may block assertion. Fricker holds it does; Hawthorne, Peet and García-Carpintero object. Indirect or sneaky assertions raise related questions about how force is fixed.
findings.quote: as soon as it is not fully determinate to the hearer what the intended content of an utterance is, or what force it is made with, the utterance fails to be assertoric
findings.note: This debate bears on whether force must be fixed at output time. It is not framed as incremental.

nearest_positions: Commitment as accountability and as answerability to challenges, with retraction as the exit — Peirce, Alston, Brandom, MacFarlane, Green
Rescorla: no norm on making assertions, only on later defend-or-retract reactions
Communicative-intention accounts making force depend on a reflexive intention at utterance — Grice, Searle, Bach & Harnish
Pagin's insufficiency objection to commitment and other hearer-directed accounts
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: LLMs and artificial speakers generally; the idea that illocutionary force is settled incrementally or retroactively through later uptake and ownership; any contrast between a force-fixing intention at output time and later commitment as what separates speakers from machines; and the claim that this is a condition on a system's organisation.

theses: Human illocutionary force is often settled incrementally through uptake and later ownership, so a force-fixing intention present at output time cannot by itself be what separates human speakers from LLMs. Whether LLMs show reason-responsive taking-up of and commitment to their earlier outputs remains open, and it is a condition on how the system is organised.
